title: Cart Check: Shopping and Money Scams Online
tagline: Before they tap "Buy," students check the storefront, the deal, the reviews, and the payment method, and they practice exactly what to do if a purchase goes wrong.
groupSize: Pairs or teams of 3; any number
overview: Online shopping scams rarely look like scams anymore. A fake storefront can have a polished design, a countdown timer, and hundreds of glowing reviews that an AI tool wrote in minutes. In this activity, students examine a mock storefront, sort real-looking shopping situations into Buy, Walk Away, or Check First, and build a four-part Cart Check: the store, the deal, the reviews, and the payment. They also weigh buy-now-pay-later plans honestly and rehearse the steps to take if they are scammed, because knowing what to do fast matters as much as avoiding the trap.
objectives: Students will apply a four-part Cart Check (store, deal, reviews, payment) to at least eight shopping situations and justify each decision.
Students will identify signs of AI-generated or fake reviews and explain why review volume and polish are not evidence of a real store.
Students will explain the payment basics that protect buyers, including secure checkout and why no legitimate seller demands gift cards or wire transfers.
Students will list, in order, the steps to take if they are scammed and compare the trade-offs of a buy-now-pay-later plan.

print: Handout A: The Kicks Vault Storefront (1 per pair)
Handout B: Buy, Walk Away, or Check First? (1 sorting mat and strip set per team, cut apart)
Handout C: My Cart Check and Scam Response Plan (1 per student)
digital: One device per pair to practice the store check on fictional search results the teacher prepares, or to look up how their own bank or card reports fraud
Optional: a generative AI chatbot your district approves, projected by the teacher only, to generate sample reviews live

prep: Print Handout A and cut Handout B into strips (one set per team). Print the Handout B key separately.

Decide how you'll handle the AI review demo. If you have an approved chatbot, test the prompt "Write 5 short five-star reviews for a sneaker store, each in a different voice" so you know what it produces. If not, Handout A's reviews serve as the example.
Remind yourself that the goal is judgment, not fear. Many online stores are legitimate; students should leave able to tell the difference and act quickly if something goes wrong.
Know whether your campus has a financial literacy course or counselor you can point students toward for follow-up questions about credit and payment plans.

steps.title: The deal of the year
steps.body: Hold up Handout A (or project it). Read the banner aloud: **"Limited drop: premium sneakers, 80% off. Only 3 pairs left. Offer ends in 09:59."** Ask: **"Hands up if you'd at least click."** Then: "What is this page doing to your brain right now?" Collect answers: urgency, scarcity, a price that feels like luck. Say: "Today you get a checklist that works even when your brain is shouting 'buy.'"
steps.note: Keep it light. Most students have seen deals like this; no one needs to share whether they have been scammed.

steps.title: Investigate the storefront
steps.body: Pairs annotate Handout A with two highlighters: **yellow** for anything that builds trust, **pink** for anything that raises doubt. Prompt them to check four places: the web address, the contact and return information, the reviews, and the payment options. Each pair writes a verdict and their top three clues at the bottom.
steps.note: Listen for "it has 1,200 reviews, so it's real." That's the misconception the review step addresses.

steps.title: Think aloud: the four-part Cart Check
steps.body: Walk through Handout A out loud using the four checks. **Store:** "Who runs this? The address is a misspelled brand-style name, there's no street address or phone, and the 'about' page is vague. I'd search the store's name plus 'reviews' or 'scam' in a new tab." **Deal:** "80% off brand-new premium shoes, with a timer, is too good to be true." **Reviews:** "Every review is five stars, posted the same week, in the same upbeat voice, praising 'the product' without saying what it was. That pattern is what AI-written or paid reviews often look like." **Payment:** "The only options are gift card, wire transfer, or a payment app 'to our manager.' That alone is a hard stop: legitimate stores don't demand gift cards."
steps.note: If you project an approved chatbot, generate five fake reviews in 20 seconds. The takeaway: reviews are cheap to fake, so check the store elsewhere.

steps.title: Sort the situations
steps.body: Teams sort the 12 strips from Handout B onto the mat: **Buy**, **Walk Away**, or **Check First**. For each, they must name which part of the Cart Check decided it (store, deal, reviews, or payment). Then reveal the key and discuss the three strips with the most disagreement.
steps.note: "Check First" is often the smartest answer. Checking means using a route you trust, such as typing the store's real address yourself or calling the number on the back of your card, never the link or number in the message.

steps.title: Pay later, pay more?
steps.body: Read strip 11 (the buy-now-pay-later offer) together. On Handout C, students list what the plan makes easier and what it can cost: late fees, several plans stacking up at once, automatic payments that can overdraw an account, and possible effects on credit depending on the provider and your payment history. Ask: **"When might a plan like this be a reasonable choice, and what would you need to check first?"**
steps.note: Avoid preaching. The honest answer is that it depends on the terms, the total you'd owe, and whether you could make every payment on time. Students should leave knowing to read the terms, not that the tool is always bad.

steps.title: If it goes wrong
steps.body: Pairs put the scam-response steps on Handout C in order and write the exact first sentence they'd say when they call their bank or card issuer. Model the sequence: **Stop paying or sending anything. Contact your bank or card issuer using the number on your card or official app. Change passwords you used on that site, and turn on two-step verification. Save evidence: screenshots, receipts, messages. Report it to the platform or marketplace and to your state's consumer protection office. Tell a trusted adult. Watch your accounts for new charges.**
steps.note: Stress that being scammed is not a personal failure. Scams are built to fool careful people, and reporting quickly can help limit the damage.

steps.title: One check I'll actually use
steps.body: Students finish on Handout C: **"The one part of the Cart Check I'll do every time, even when I'm in a hurry, is… because…"** A few volunteers share.
steps.note: Look for a specific check, like "I'll search the store name plus 'scam' before paying," not "be careful."

unplugged: Everything runs on paper. Handout A is the storefront, Handout B is a hands-on sort, and Handout C is the plan. For the lateral store check, give each team a printed "search results" slip from the key describing what a search for the store's name would turn up. The fake-review demo works by comparing Handout A's reviews side by side and naming the patterns.
digital: Pairs practice the store check by searching the fictional store name (it returns nothing, which is itself a clue) and then look up how their own bank, credit union, or card issuer tells customers to report fraud, noting the official route. In an LMS, post Handout A as an image and run Handout B as a drag-and-drop sort. Only the teacher uses an AI chatbot, on the projector, to show how fast convincing reviews can be generated.
whyTech: Watching an AI tool write a page of believable five-star reviews in seconds makes the lesson stick in a way a printed review never can: students see that review volume proves nothing. Finding their own bank's real fraud-reporting route gives them a step they can use the same day.

adaptations.label: Higher Ed
adaptations.text: Add strips on rental listings and textbook resale scams, and extend the payment discussion to how card disputes and chargebacks generally work and why reading the terms matters.

adaptations.label: Grades 6–8
adaptations.text: Use the storefront and strips 1–8, focus on game currency and in-app purchases, and replace the buy-now-pay-later step with "ask the adult who owns the card."

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Pre-teach deal, review, refund, checkout, and scam with icons, and let pairs annotate Handout A in their strongest language before sharing in English.

adaptations.label: Family connection
adaptations.text: Send Handout C's Cart Check home and invite students to run it with a family member on a real purchase they are considering.

lookFors: Handout A annotations name at least one clue in each of the four areas: store, deal, reviews, payment.
Students explain that a large number of polished reviews is not proof of a real store, and describe at least one pattern that suggests AI-written or paid reviews.
Every student can state that no legitimate seller demands payment by gift card or wire transfer, and names a safer payment route.
Scam-response steps on Handout C are in a sensible order and begin with stopping payment and contacting the bank through a trusted route.
reflection: How do I protect my money and personal information when I shop online? (Student ELE S2.1)
What made the fake store convincing, and which check would have caught it fastest?
When AI can write a thousand believable reviews, what evidence of a real store should I look for instead?
transfer: Next lesson, students apply the Cart Check to a sponsored social media ad or a marketplace listing and present their verdict in 60 seconds. At home, they share the "If it goes wrong" steps with someone in their family who shops online.

connections.title: Family App Privacy Audit
connections.note: A natural follow-up on what shopping and payment apps collect.

connections.title: News Literacy Project
connections.note: Lessons on persuasion, sponsored content, and checking claims online.

handouts.title: The Kicks Vault Storefront
handouts.instructions: This store is fictional. Highlight trust-builders in yellow and doubt-raisers in pink. Check the address, contact and returns, reviews, and payment.
paragraphs: **Web address:** kicksvault-officiall-outlet.shop. **Banner:** "LIMITED DROP: Premium sneakers 80% OFF. Only 3 pairs left! Offer ends in 09:59." A countdown timer ticks at the top of every page.

**Featured item:** Stratos Runner Elite, usually $220, now $39.99. "100% authentic, straight from the factory. Free shipping worldwide." The product photos have different backgrounds and lighting, and one still shows another store's watermark in the corner.

**About us:** "Kicks Vault is a passionate team dedicated to bringing you the best quality at the best price. Customer satisfaction is our top priority." There is no street address, no phone number, and no company name. The only contact is a web form.
**Returns:** "All sales final on discounted items. Returns accepted within 7 days for store credit only, after approval."

**Reviews (1,284 reviews, 5.0 stars):** "Amazing product!! Fast shipping and great quality, will buy again!" (Posted 3 days ago) · "I love this product so much, it exceeded all my expectations. Highly recommend this store to everyone!" (Posted 3 days ago) · "Great quality product at an unbeatable price. The customer service was excellent and very helpful!" (Posted 4 days ago) · "Absolutely perfect, just as described, five stars, thank you Kicks Vault!" (Posted 4 days ago)

**Checkout:** "To keep prices low, we accept: gift cards (enter card numbers below), wire transfer, or send payment through a payment app directly to our store manager, Kevin." The checkout page address begins with "http" rather than "https," and the browser shows a "Not secure" warning.

**Search results slip (for the unplugged lateral check):** A search for "Kicks Vault outlet" turns up no news coverage or business listing. A consumer forum thread from last week titled "Kicks Vault never shipped my order" has several replies saying the same thing, and the store's web address was registered last month.

handouts.title: Buy, Walk Away, or Check First?
handouts.instructions: Cut apart the strips. Place each on the mat, and name which part of the Cart Check decided it: store, deal, reviews, or payment.

items.text: 1. A seller on a local marketplace app says your concert tickets are ready, but you must pay with three $50 gift cards and send photos of the card numbers.
items.why: Payment: no legitimate seller demands gift cards. Photos of the card numbers are the same as handing over cash.

items.text: 2. You type the address of a well-known bookstore chain yourself, the checkout page shows https, and you pay with a credit card. The price is a normal sale price.
items.why: Store, deal, and payment all check out: known store reached by a route you trust, realistic price, secure checkout.

items.text: 3. A text says your package from ParcelPoint couldn't be delivered and asks you to tap a link and pay a $1.99 redelivery fee.
items.why: Store: don't use the link. Open the carrier's real app or type its address yourself to check the tracking number.

items.text: 4. A gaming headset listed at 90% off on a site you've never heard of, with a timer and only one payment option: cryptocurrency.
items.why: Deal and payment: an extreme discount plus a pressure timer plus a hard-to-reverse payment is a classic scam pattern.

items.text: 5. A small online shop has 40 reviews spread across two years, some four stars and some three, with photos and complaints about slow shipping. It lists a street address and phone number.
items.why: Reviews: mixed ratings over time with specific details look like real customers. Store: contact information you can verify.

items.text: 6. A new shop has 900 five-star reviews, all posted this week, all with nearly the same wording and none mentioning what was bought.
items.why: Reviews: identical tone, same week, and no specifics are signs of generated or paid reviews. Search the store elsewhere before any purchase.

items.text: 7. An influencer you follow posts a discount code for a skincare brand. The post is tagged #ad and links to the brand's own site.
items.why: Store and deal: a paid ad isn't a scam by itself, but search the brand's reputation and return policy before buying.

items.text: 8. A "seller" on a resale app asks you to move the conversation to a private messaging app and pay outside the platform to "avoid fees."
items.why: Payment: leaving the platform removes its buyer protection. Pay only inside the app.

items.text: 9. A pop-up says you've won a free phone and need to pay only $4.95 shipping with your card number.
items.why: Deal: a prize you never entered is bait. Small fees are often used to collect card numbers for bigger charges.

items.text: 10. An email that looks like it's from your favorite clothing store offers 30% off, but the sender address is a string of random letters.
items.why: Store: the offer might be real. Type the store's address yourself or open its app to see if the sale exists.

items.text: 11. At checkout, a store offers to split a $240 order into four payments of $60 every two weeks. You already have two other pay-later plans going.
items.why: Payment: read the terms for late fees and automatic payments, and add up everything you already owe before saying yes.

items.text: 12. A classmate shares a link to a site selling last year's calculator model at a normal used price. The site has a real business address, a clear return policy, and secure checkout.
items.why: All four checks pass. Legitimate deals exist; the Cart Check helps you trust them for good reasons.

handouts.title: My Cart Check and Scam Response Plan
handouts.instructions: Keep this plan. Don't write real card numbers, passwords, or account details anywhere on it.

sections.prompt: The four-part Cart Check in my own words. One question for each: Store · Deal · Reviews · Payment.

Payment basics: what I look for at checkout, and the payment methods I'll never use with a stranger (and why):
